seoul: Most international flights land at Incheon Airport. The AREX train reaches Seoul Station in about an hour, and airport limousine buses stop near most big hotels. Flights from Japan and China also use Gimpo Airport, which is on the subway. See our guide to getting from Incheon Airport to Seoul.

Three days covers the palaces, a market, a hanok neighbourhood and one evening view. Five days lets you add a day trip, such as the DMZ, Suwon or Nami Island, and slow down in neighbourhoods like Seongsu or Yeonnam-dong.

The subway reaches almost everywhere, with signs and announcements in English. Get a T-money card at any convenience store, top it up with cash and tap in and out. Taxis are good value for short trips, especially at night, and Kakao T works for foreigners.

April and May, and late September to early November, are the most comfortable months. Summer is hot, humid and rainy; winter is cold and dry but bright, with fewer crowds and Christmas lights in December.

First-time visitors usually stay around Myeongdong or Jongno for sightseeing, Hongdae for nightlife and a younger feel, or Gangnam for business and shopping. Being close to a subway station matters more than the exact district.

Gyeongbokgung Palace and the Bukchon hanok streets next to it make the classic first morning; visitors wearing hanbok get into the palaces free. Changdeokgung's Secret Garden needs a guided-tour ticket, so book or arrive early. In the afternoon, walk the Cheonggyecheon stream to Gwangjang Market, then finish with a view from N Seoul Tower or a Han River park at sunset.

Start at a market: Gwangjang Market for bindaetteok (mung bean pancakes) and mayak gimbap, Myeongdong's evening street stalls for skewers and egg bread. Korean barbecue, samgyetang (ginseng chicken soup) and a late-night fried chicken and beer are all easy to find in any busy neighbourhood. Many restaurants have picture menus or tablets with an English option.

Most places take foreign cards, but keep some cash for markets and to top up T-money. Download Naver Map or KakaoMap before you arrive, as Google Maps does not give walking or driving directions in Korea. Palaces and many museums close one day a week, usually Monday or Tuesday, so check before you go.
busan: The KTX train runs from Seoul Station to Busan Station in about two and a half to three hours. Gimhae Airport has domestic flights from Seoul and Jeju and some international routes, and is linked to the city by light rail and bus.

Two or three days is enough for the beaches, Gamcheon Culture Village, Haedong Yonggungsa temple and Jagalchi fish market without rushing. Busan also works as the last stop of a one-week trip from Seoul via Gyeongju.

Busan has a subway with four main lines, and the same T-money card you use in Seoul works here. The sights are spread along the coast, so expect some longer rides; buses and taxis fill the gaps, especially for the temple and the hillside villages.

Busan is a few degrees milder than Seoul in winter. July and August are beach season, lively but crowded. Spring and autumn are the best for walking the coastal paths, and early October brings the Busan International Film Festival.
Haeundae is the classic beach base with big hotels; Gwangalli has the bridge view and a lively bar scene; Seomyeon and Nampo are central and good for food, markets and transport.

Spend one day on the east side: Haeundae Beach, the Blueline Park sky capsules or beach train along the coast, and Haedong Yonggungsa, a temple built on the rocks above the sea. Spend another in the old centre: Jagalchi fish market, BIFF Square, Gukje Market and the colourful hillside houses of Gamcheon Culture Village. In the evening, the Gwangan Bridge lights up over Gwangalli Beach.

Busan is known for dwaeji gukbap (pork and rice soup), milmyeon (cold wheat noodles, a local take on naengmyeon), and very fresh raw fish at Jagalchi, where you choose your fish downstairs and eat it upstairs. Ssiat hotteok, a sweet pancake filled with seeds, is the street snack to try around BIFF Square.

Distances along the coast are longer than they look on a map, so group sights by area. Beaches are busiest on summer weekends and during the July and August holidays. Taxis are a good shortcut up the steep roads to Gamcheon and between the temple and Haeundae.
jeju: Flights from Seoul Gimpo to Jeju take about an hour and run all day; there are also flights from Busan and other cities, and some international routes. Ferries exist from the south coast but take much longer.

Three or four days lets you see the east (Seongsan Ilchulbong and the coast), the west (beaches and tea fields) and the south (waterfalls around Seogwipo), with one day for Hallasan or a slower walk on an Olle trail.

Renting a car is the easiest way to see the island; you need an International Driving Permit. Buses reach most sights from Jeju City and Seogwipo but are slower and less frequent. Taxis are useful for short hops.

Jeju is milder than the mainland but very windy, especially in winter. Canola flowers and cherry blossoms come in late March and early April, summer is beach season, and autumn brings silver grass on the volcanic hills. Strong winds can delay flights, so keep a little slack in your plans.
Jeju City is close to the airport and practical for short stays. Seogwipo in the south suits waterfalls and the southern coast. Staying in the east or west for a night or two saves driving time.

Climb Seongsan Ilchulbong, the volcanic crater on the east coast, ideally at sunrise. Walk a section of the Olle trail along the south coast near Seogwipo, with Jeongbang and Cheonjiyeon waterfalls nearby. On the west side, Hyeopjae Beach has pale sand and clear turquoise water, and the green tea fields around Osulloc are a calm stop. Fit enthusiasts can climb Hallasan, South Korea's highest mountain, starting early in the morning.

Jeju black pork, grilled at the table, is the island's signature meal. Seafood is everywhere: try haemul ttukbaegi (seafood stew), abalone porridge, and dishes made from the catch of the haenyeo, the island's women divers. Hallabong, a sweet local citrus, appears in juices, desserts and gifts.

Jeju is visa-free for many nationalities under its own rules; check the current conditions before you fly. Weather changes quickly, especially on Hallasan, so bring a wind layer in every season. Hallasan's summit trails need a free advance reservation, and trails close early in the day.
gyeongju: The KTX goes from Seoul Station to Singyeongju Station in about two hours, and from there buses run to the old town centre. Gyeongju is also an easy day trip or overnight stop from Busan by train or intercity bus.

One full day covers the royal tombs, Cheomseongdae, Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond at night and Hwangnidan-gil. Stay a second day for Bulguksa temple and Seokguram grotto on the hillside east of town.
The historic centre is flat and walkable, and renting a bicycle is popular. City buses reach Bulguksa and the station; taxis are handy for the hill to Seokguram.
Cherry blossoms around the tombs and Bomun Lake in early April and the autumn leaves in late October and November are the highlights. Summers are hot; winter is quiet and cold but clear.
Stay near Hwangnidan-gil or the tomb park to walk to the night views, in a hanok guesthouse for the atmosphere, or at Bomun Lake for larger resort hotels.

Gyeongju was the capital of the Silla kingdom for nearly a thousand years and is sometimes called a museum without walls. Walk among the grassy royal tombs of Daereungwon, see Cheomseongdae observatory, and visit Donggung Palace and Wolji Pond in the evening, when the pavilions are lit and reflected in the water. Bulguksa temple and Seokguram grotto, both UNESCO-listed, are on the hillside east of town.

Gyeongju bread (Hwangnam-ppang), a small pastry filled with sweet red bean, is the famous souvenir snack. Ssambap restaurants near the tombs serve rice with a table full of side dishes and leaves for wrapping. Hwangnidan-gil has cafes and small restaurants in old hanok buildings.

The main sights are close together in town, but Bulguksa and Seokguram are a bus or taxi ride away. Gyeongju National Museum is free and a good way to understand the Silla treasures before you see the sites. Hotels at Bomun Lake are quieter but further from the old town.
jeonju: KTX trains run from Seoul (Yongsan) to Jeonju Station in under two hours, and express buses from Seoul take about two and a half to three hours. From the station or bus terminal, a short taxi ride reaches the hanok village.
One day covers the Hanok Village, Gyeonggijeon Shrine, Jeondong Cathedral and the food. Stay overnight to see the village lit up in the evening and visit Nambu Market's night stalls on weekends.
The hanok village and the old town are compact and best on foot. Taxis and city buses are easy for the station and other districts.
Spring and autumn are pleasant for walking; weekends and holidays are busy, so go early in the day. Jeonju is famous for bibimbap and street food at any time of year.
Sleeping in a hanok guesthouse inside the village is the experience most visitors come for; expect floor mattresses and paper doors. Hotels outside the village are cheaper and quieter.

Jeonju Hanok Village has more than 600 traditional houses, many now guesthouses, cafes and craft shops. Gyeonggijeon Shrine holds a portrait of King Taejo, the founder of the Joseon dynasty, and Jeondong Cathedral stands right opposite. Climb to Omokdae for a view over the tiled roofs, then walk to Nambu Market.

Jeonju is famous as the home of bibimbap, served with many toppings in a hot or brass bowl. Kongnamul gukbap, a bean sprout soup eaten for breakfast and hangovers, is the other local dish. On weekend evenings, the night market at Nambu Market sells street food, and the youth mall upstairs has small restaurants and bars.

The hanok village gets very busy on weekends and holidays; arrive in the morning or stay the night to enjoy it quietly. Hanbok rental shops line the main streets. Jeonju is also a good base for a day trip to Maisan and its temple of stone towers.
gangneung: The KTX runs from Seoul Station and Cheongnyangni to Gangneung in about two hours. Express buses from Seoul take a little longer.
One day covers Gyeongpo Beach and lake, Anmok's coffee street and Ojukheon; stay overnight for a sunrise at Jeongdongjin or Gyeongpo.
City buses and taxis connect the station, beaches and sights. Distances between the beaches are short by taxi.
Summer is beach season. Winter is cold but bright, and the east coast is the classic place to watch the first sunrise of the year on 1 January. Spring brings cherry blossoms around Gyeongpo Lake.
Stay near Gyeongpo Beach for the sea and the lake, or near the station for easy trains.

Gangneung sits on the east coast where the mountains meet the sea. Gyeongpo Beach and Gyeongpo Lake are side by side, with Gyeongpodae pavilion above the lake. Ojukheon is the birthplace of the scholar Yi I, whose face is on the 5,000 won note. Jeongdongjin, a short trip south, is famous for its seaside train station and sunrise views.

Anmok Beach has a long row of coffee shops facing the sea, and Gangneung is often called Korea's coffee city. Chodang sundubu, soft tofu made with seawater in Chodang village, is the local speciality, served plain or in a spicy stew. The central market has fresh seafood and local snacks.

Since the 2018 Winter Olympics, the KTX has made Gangneung an easy weekend trip from Seoul, so trains fill up on Fridays and holidays; book ahead. Beaches are crowded in late July and August. The coast is often windy in winter, but the skies are usually clear.
incheon: Incheon is next to Seoul and home to Korea's main international airport. Subway Line 1 and the Suin-Bundang line link central Incheon with Seoul, and the AREX train runs between the airport and Seoul.
Half a day or a day is enough for Chinatown, the Fairy Tale Village and Wolmido, or Songdo's Central Park. It also makes a good first or last night close to the airport.
The subway covers the main areas and the same T-money card works as in Seoul. Taxis are useful for the airport island and the coast.
Any time of year. Songdo and the waterfront are pleasant on spring and autumn evenings.
Choose the airport area or Unseo for early flights, Songdo for modern hotels, or central Incheon for easy access to Seoul.

Incheon Chinatown, Korea's oldest, is the home of jjajangmyeon (black bean noodles), and the Fairy Tale Village next door has painted alleys. Wolmido has a seaside promenade and small amusement rides. Songdo Central Park, with its canal and modern skyline, is pleasant in the evening. Ganghwa Island to the north has dolmen sites and temples.

Try jjajangmyeon and jjamppong (spicy seafood noodle soup) in Chinatown, and the Jjajangmyeon Museum there explains how the dish became a Korean favourite. Sinpo International Market is known for dakgangjeong, crispy sweet and spicy fried chicken. Seafood restaurants line the waterfront at Wolmido and Yeonan Pier.

Incheon Airport has a transit tour programme for long layovers and a free Korean culture area, so even a short stop can include a little sightseeing. If you have an early flight, staying near the airport saves a long trip from central Seoul.
sokcho: Express buses from Seoul reach Sokcho in about two and a half to three hours. It is also an easy bus or taxi ride from Gangneung, an hour or so down the coast.
One or two days: a day for Seoraksan National Park and another for the seafront, Abai Village and the markets.
Local buses run to Seoraksan's main entrance and along the coast; taxis are quick around town.
Mid to late October is the peak for autumn leaves in Seoraksan, and the park is very busy then. Summer brings beach crowds; winter is cold, quiet and good for sunrise views over the East Sea.
Stay by the beach or the port for the sea and the markets, or near Seoraksan's entrance if you want an early start on the trails.

Seoraksan National Park is the main reason most people come: take the cable car toward Gwongeumseong fortress for a view with little effort, or hike to Ulsanbawi rock if you are fit. In town, a small hand-pulled ferry crosses to Abai Village, settled by refugees from the North during the Korean War. Naksansa temple stands on a cliff above the sea a short ride south.

Sokcho Tourist and Fishery Market (Jungang Market) is the place for dakgangjeong, crispy sweet fried chicken sold in boxes, and for fresh seafood. Abai Village is known for squid sundae, squid stuffed with rice and vegetables, and for naengmyeon. Mulhoe, a cold spicy raw fish soup, is a summer favourite along the coast.

Seoraksan's autumn colours peak in mid to late October, and the park is extremely busy then, especially at weekends; go on a weekday and start early. Some higher trails close during dry seasons for fire prevention. Sokcho also makes a good two-day trip combined with Gangneung by bus along the coast.
yeosu: The KTX runs from Seoul (Yongsan) to Yeosu Expo Station in about three hours. Yeosu Airport has domestic flights from Seoul.
One or two days covers the sea cable car, Odongdo island and the waterfront at night, with time for seafood and Hyangiram Hermitage at sunrise.
City buses and taxis connect the station, the harbour and the main sights.
Spring and autumn are the most pleasant. Yeosu is known for its night sea views, so plan at least one evening on the waterfront.
Stay near the Expo area or the harbour for walking to the night views and restaurants.

Ride the Yeosu Maritime Cable Car across the harbour, with glass-floored cabins if you want a thrill. Odongdo is a small island linked by a long causeway, covered in camellia trees that flower in late winter and early spring. Hyangiram Hermitage clings to cliffs above the sea and is one of Korea's best-known sunrise spots.

Yeosu is famous for gejang, raw crab marinated in soy sauce or a spicy sauce, often served as an all-you-can-eat set with rice. Seafood is the focus everywhere, from grilled fish to octopus. Dolsan gat kimchi, made with a local mustard leaf, is a speciality to try or take home.

Yeosu's 'night sea' is celebrated in a well-known Korean pop song, and the waterfront around Jongpo and the Romantic Pocha street is busy on summer evenings. Hyangiram is a short climb up steps from the bus stop; allow time if you go for sunrise. Suncheon Bay wetland and its reed fields are an easy trip from Yeosu.
daegu: The KTX takes about one hour forty minutes from Seoul to Dongdaegu Station. Daegu is also about an hour from Busan by train.
One or two days for Seomun Market, the old town alleys, Kim Gwang-seok Street and a view from Apsan Park, with good food throughout.
Daegu has subway and monorail lines that cover the main areas; taxis are inexpensive.
Daegu is one of the hottest cities in Korea in summer. Spring and autumn are the most comfortable months to explore on foot.
Stay in the central Jung-gu area near the markets and old town, or near Dongdaegu Station for easy trains.

Seomun Market is one of Korea's largest traditional markets, with a busy night market in the warmer months. The old town has the Modern History Alleys, with Gyesan Cathedral and the 90 steps of the March First Movement trail. Kim Gwang-seok Street is a mural lane dedicated to a much-loved folk singer, and Apsan Park's cable car leads to a viewpoint over the city.

Daegu is known for makchang (grilled pork intestines), jjimgalbi (spicy braised beef ribs) on Dongin-dong's jjimgalbi alley, and napjak mandu, flat dumplings. Seomun Market's food stalls serve kalguksu (knife-cut noodles) and other quick, cheap meals.

Daegu is often the hottest city in Korea in July and August, so plan sightseeing for mornings and evenings. Palgongsan mountain and Donghwasa temple are an easy bus ride north of the centre. The city is also a good stop between Seoul and Busan, and Gyeongju is under an hour away.
daejeon: Daejeon is about an hour from Seoul by KTX, with two main stations, Daejeon and Seodaejeon.
A day trip or one night is enough for the science museums, Hanbat Arboretum and the city's famous bakery.
A subway line and buses cover the city; taxis are easy to find.
Any season; spring and autumn are the best for the parks and arboretum.
Stay near Daejeon Station or in the Dunsan area for restaurants and transport.

Daejeon is Korea's science city. Expo Science Park and the National Science Museum are good with children, and Hanbat Arboretum nearby is a large, free city garden. Yuseong is known for its hot springs, with free foot baths in the street. Gyejoksan's red clay trail is a popular barefoot walk.

Sungsimdang, a bakery founded in 1956, is the city's most famous food stop, known for its fried soboro bread and seasonal fruit cakes; expect queues. Kalguksu (knife-cut noodles) is a local favourite, with many long-running restaurants downtown.

Daejeon is a convenient base or stopover in the middle of the country: the KTX reaches it in about an hour from Seoul, and Gongju and Buyeo, the old Baekje capitals, are close by bus. Daejeon's main sights are spread out, so the subway and taxis are useful.
gwangju: The KTX runs from Seoul (Yongsan) to Gwangju Songjeong Station in about two hours.
One or two days for the Asia Culture Center, the May 18 memorial sites, Yangnim-dong's old houses and the food. Damyang's bamboo forest is an easy half-day trip.
Gwangju has a subway line and a good bus network; taxis are inexpensive.
Spring and autumn are the most comfortable. Gwangju is known as one of Korea's best food cities at any time of year.
Stay downtown near the Asia Culture Center for walking to sights and restaurants, or near Songjeong Station for trains.

Gwangju is the city of the May 18 Democratic Uprising of 1980. The May 18 National Cemetery and the memorial sites downtown tell that story, and the Asia Culture Center hosts exhibitions and performances. Yangnim-dong has early 20th-century missionary houses and the Penguin Village alley of folk art. Mudeungsan, a national park on the city's edge, offers rocky ridges and good hiking.

The Jeolla region is known for generous tables, and Gwangju restaurants often serve many side dishes with every meal. Try tteokgalbi (grilled minced short rib patties), especially in nearby Songjeong or Damyang, and Gwangju's oritang, a hearty duck soup.

Damyang's Juknokwon bamboo forest and its tree-lined Metasequoia road are an easy half-day trip by bus. The Gwangju Biennale, one of Asia's major contemporary art events, is usually held in the autumn of even-numbered years.
